title: The name chanted
hookLine: Namo Amituofo chanted as people walk around a Chinese hall

cards: What happens to a name when you say it with every step? In a Buddhist hall in China, a line of people in gray robes and ordinary coats moves slowly around the room.

Slippers on a wooden floor, hands folded or holding beads. The line curves past a golden figure of a Buddha and around again, everyone saying the same short phrase in a soft, even chant: Namo Amituofo.
A step, a syllable, a step. Nobody is going anywhere, and nobody seems in a hurry to stop.

teach.b: First, whose name. Amituofo is how Chinese Buddhists say Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light.
In the Pure Land sutras, he made vows long ago to create a land where beings could practice without obstacles, and to welcome those who call on him with trust.
Pure Land Buddhists, in China and across East Asia, rest their practice on that vow. Second, the words.
Namo means homage, or I turn to: a greeting and a turning, homage to Amitabha. Some Chinese Buddhists use the phrase in daily life too, to say hello, thank you, or I'm sorry. Third, the walking.

teach.h: AROUND THE HALL, BUDDHA ON THE RIGHT.
teach.b: People circle the image of the Buddha, keeping it on their right side, an old Buddhist sign of respect. They chant as they go, slow, sometimes quicker, then slow again.
Then they often sit, and the chanting goes on silently, inside. Fourth, why walk.

The body walks, the voice chants, and the name gives the mind somewhere to rest. In the shorter Pure Land sutra, the Buddha tells his disciple Shariputra about those who hold the name of Amitabha with an undivided mind.
Teachers in this school differ on how much the practice is trust in Amitabha's vow and how much it is steadying the mind; some hold both together. For them, the name isn't a magic word.
It's a way of remembering, again and again, with feet and voice.

how: Pure Land Buddhists in China and across East Asia recite Amitabha's name, often on beads, and in temple halls they walk in a line around the Buddha image chanting Namo Amituofo, then sit while the recitation continues silently.

games.q: you're walking in the line around the hall, chanting the name, and your mind drifts to tonight's dinner. what do you do?
o: step out of the line until your head is clear.
notice your next step and return to the name.
games.why: the walk is built for this. each step is a fresh chance to come back to the name.

practice: If you have room, walk slowly in a small loop around a table or the edge of a rug; if not, sit and press one foot, then the other, into the floor.
With each step, say a syllable softly or in your head, na, mo, a, mi, tuo, fo, or simply step, step. When the mind wanders, notice where your foot is, and return.

wordCard.voice: The name chanted. Namo Amituofo, homage to Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light, said with each step as people walk around a hall. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit Amitabha, boundless light: the Buddha whose name Chinese Buddhists chant as Amituofo.

carryVoice: Your line: walking the name. Feet, voice and mind, all going the same way. Until tomorrow.
